failures.title: Jeep EGD 3.6 Pentastar Engine Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: Oil cooler / filter housing failure - shared with earlier Pentastars
items.whatHappens: The combined oil cooler and oil filter housing is made of plastic. Repeated heat cycles make it brittle; cracks develop, leading to oil leaks that pool in the V of the engine and drip down the back. The leak can be oil, coolant, or both. Overtightening the oil filter cap during changes (spec is only 18 ft-lb) accelerates failure .
items.repairVsReplace: The housing itself can be replaced - many owners upgrade to an aftermarket aluminium housing (£300-£600) which eliminates the problem permanently. If the leak has been ignored and oil pressure has dropped, bearing damage may have occurred, requiring a full engine replacement.

items.title: Rocker arm and lifter failure - the "Pentastar Tick"
items.whatHappens: Faulty rocker arms and lifters cause a ticking noise (especially on cold start) that can progress to misfires, reduced power, and eventually camshaft damage if ignored. The failure appears more common on the right cylinder bank, suggesting an oil flow design issue .
items.repairVsReplace: Rocker arm and lifter replacement is a top-end job (£800-£1,500 at an independent). If left until the camshaft is damaged, costs rise significantly. Full engine replacement is rarely needed unless oil starvation has occurred.

items.title: Camshaft phaser issues - earlier EGD models
items.whatHappens: Some EGD engines have experienced camshaft phaser wear, leading to timing-related codes and reduced performance. While less common than on the earlier ERC, it remains a documented issue on 2018-2020 production examples .
items.repairVsReplace: Phaser replacement is a significant job requiring timing chain removal (£1,200-£2,000). If ignored, timing chain failure can result.

failures.goodYearsLine: The EGD (2018+) benefits from the ongoing refinement of the Pentastar platform; the early cylinder-head issues of 2011-2013 are not present. However, the oil cooler housing remains a weak point across all years. Later builds (2021+) have received further revisions, though long-term reliability data is still emerging.

variants.title: How to Confirm You Have the EGD 3.6 Pentastar
variants.intro: The EGD is one of several codes in Chrysler's Pentastar V6 family. The EGD designation typically indicates the updated 3.6L Pentastar used from 2018 onward, with revisions including improved piston rings, updated VVL hardware, and emissions refinements. In some applications, the EGD is paired with the eTorque mild-hybrid system. Where to find the engine code: - On the engine block - a stamped label on the front-left side of the V6 (looking from the front) - On the V5C registration document under "Engine number" - On the driver's door pillar or under-bonnet VIN/engine sticker - Via a VIN decoder - enter your full 17-digit VIN online to confirm the factory engine code Common confusions: | Similar code | Difference | Link | |--------------|------------|------| | ERC | Earlier Pentastar (2016-2018) - the EGD is the updated variant with revised internals | [ERC engine] (see previous page) | | ERB | Earlier Pentastar (2011-2015); left-cylinder-head misfire issues more common | [ERB engine] | | EHB | 2.0L Hurricane - completely different engine (inline-4 vs V6) | [EHB engine] (see previous page) | | EXF | 3.0 EcoDiesel - completely different engine | [EXF engine] (see previous page) |

buyingGuide.title: Buying a Replacement EGD 3.6 Pentastar - What to Choose

options.label: Used
options.body: A used EGD can make sense for older Grand Cherokee or Wrangler examples where vehicle value doesn't justify a recon unit. However - insist on documented service history and evidence that the oil cooler housing has been replaced or isn't leaking. The "Pentastar Tick" (rocker arm noise) is a red flag on any used unit; walk away if you hear it on cold start. Given the relative newness of the EGD (2018+), many used units will be lower-mileage, but check for the oil cooler issue regardless.

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: A proper EGD recon addresses the oil cooler housing (often upgraded to aluminium), replaces rocker arms and lifters, checks camshaft phasers, and renews all gaskets and seals. This is the sweet spot for most UK owners - the failure-prone components are addressed, you get 12-24 months warranty, and cost is far below a new unit. Given the EGD's age profile, a reconditioned unit with upgraded components is often a better investment than a low-mileage used engine with unknown history.

options.label: Rebuilt
options.body: A full rebuild of the EGD is rarely needed unless the engine has suffered oil starvation from an ignored cooler leak, leading to bottom-end damage. If rebuilding, specify upgraded aluminium oil cooler housing, new timing chain and guides, and full rocker/lifter replacement. This is the "zero-risk" option for high-value Wrangler Rubicon or Grand Cherokee Overland examples.

buyingGuide.supplyFitLine: Fitting through our network of vetted UK Jeep specialists - supply-only or full supply and fit, with nationwide delivery and warranty cover on every reconditioned and rebuilt unit.
buyingGuide.vehicleValueNote: The EGD sits in vehicles with wide value ranges - a 2018 Grand Cherokee may be worth £12,000-£18,000, while a 2023 Wrangler Rubicon can exceed £40,000. For most applications, the vehicle value comfortably exceeds replacement cost. For lower-value examples (sub-£10,000), a used engine with documented oil cooler history may be the most financially sensible route. For higher-value or off-road-use vehicles, a reconditioned unit with upgraded oil cooler is the better long-term investment. Always evaluate the specific vehicle's condition and value before committing to a replacement.

items.question: What is the most common failure on the Jeep EGD 3.6 Pentastar engine?
items.answer: The most common failure is the plastic oil cooler / filter housing, which cracks and leaks oil or coolant into the V of the engine - this issue carries over from earlier Pentastar variants. Typical onset is 40,000-100,000 miles. The fix is housing replacement; many owners upgrade to an aluminium unit (£300-£600) to prevent recurrence. If ignored, oil pressure drops can cause bottom-end bearing failure, requiring a full engine replacement.

items.question: What is the difference between the EGD and ERC Pentastar engines?
items.answer: The EGD is the updated version of the Pentastar V6, introduced in 2018 with revisions including improved piston rings, updated VVL hardware, and emissions refinements. The ERC (2016-2018) is the direct predecessor with similar power output but earlier internal specifications. Both share the oil cooler housing weak point. The EGD is generally considered more refined, but the oil cooler remains a concern across both. Browse reconditioned EGD engines with warranty.

items.question: Should I buy a used or reconditioned EGD engine?
items.answer: A used EGD is viable only if it has full documented service history and evidence that the oil cooler housing has been replaced or isn't leaking - the "Pentastar Tick" (rocker arm noise) is a red flag on any used unit. Given the EGD's relative newness (2018+), many used units will be lower-mileage, but check for the oil cooler issue regardless. A reconditioned unit is the better choice for most owners, as it addresses the oil cooler (often upgraded to aluminium), replaces rocker arms and lifters, and includes a 12-24 month warranty. Browse reconditioned EGD engines with warranty.

items.question: How do I confirm my Jeep has the EGD engine code?
items.answer: Check three places: the engine block itself (a stamped label on the front-left side of the V6), your V5C registration document under 'Engine number' (the EGD code appears in the first three characters), and use a VIN decoder online with your full 17-digit VIN to pull the factory build sheet. Given the confusion with other 3.6 Pentastar codes (ERC, ERB), always verify the physical label before ordering.
